paraphrase: An established tenet (siddhānta) is a position settled on the basis of a system, a presupposition or an admission; it is of four kinds — common to all systems (sarvatantra), peculiar to one system (pratitantra), one whose establishment establishes others (adhikaraṇa), and one accepted provisionally in order to examine its details (abhyupagama) — each of which the sūtras define.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: Proposition (pratijñā), reason (hetu), example (udāharaṇa), application (upanaya) and conclusion (nigamana) are the members (avayava).

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: The proposition states what is to be proved; the reason proves it through similarity to the example, or likewise through dissimilarity; the example is a familiar instance that, being similar to what is to be proved, possesses its property — or, in the contrary case, the opposite; the application restates the subject as being 'so' (or 'not so') with reference to the example; the conclusion repeats the proposition on the ground of the stated reason.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: Hypothetical reasoning (tarka) is a reasoned consideration (ūha), for the sake of knowing the truth, about a thing whose nature is not known, by examining which causes (explanations) are fitting.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: The pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa) are the inconclusive (savyabhicāra), the contradictory (viruddha), the one that leaves the question open (prakaraṇasama), the one that itself needs proof (sādhyasama) and the mistimed (kālātīta).

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: The inconclusive reason strays (from what is to be proved); the contradictory is one that opposes the very tenet it was adopted to support; the prakaraṇasama, put forward to settle a question, gives rise to the same deliberation; the sādhyasama does not differ from what is to be proved, since it too needs proof; the kālātīta is one adduced after its time has passed.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The meaning of 'kālātīta' (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) is explained differently by the commentators.

paraphrase: A quibble (chala) is the countering of a statement by supposing an alternative meaning; it is of three kinds — verbal (vākchala), generalizing (sāmānyacchala) and figurative (upacāracchala); the sūtras define each and reject the objection that the figurative quibble is only a verbal one.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: A futile rejoinder (jāti) is an objection made merely on the ground of similarity or dissimilarity.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: A point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is misunderstanding (vipratipatti) or non-understanding (apratipatti).

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: An opponent holds that perception and the other means of knowledge are not valid, since they can be established neither before, nor after, nor together with their objects; it is replied that by the same reasoning the denial itself would be impossible, that a denial of all means of knowledge undermines itself, and that if the denial is valid not all means of knowledge are refuted.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: A means of knowledge can also be an object of knowledge, as a balance is both instrument and object of weighing; to the objection that establishing means of knowledge by means of knowledge leads to an infinite regress, it is replied that their establishment is like the establishment of a lamp's light.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 2.1.19 reads: na pradīpaprakāśasiddhivat tatsiddheḥ. How the lamp analogy works is explained by the Bhāṣya; the identification of the opponent with Nāgārjuna (whose Vigrahavyāvartanī attacks the lamp analogy) is a scholarly hypothesis, not the commentators' statement.

paraphrase: Against the view that perception is really inference, since only a part of a thing is ever grasped, the sūtras hold that the whole (avayavin) is grasped as something over and above its parts: otherwise nothing would be grasped at all, and a thing could not be held or pulled as one; the objection that wholes are grasped the way an army or a forest is (as aggregates) fails, because atoms are beyond the senses.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 2.1.30.

paraphrase: The objection that inference is not a means of knowledge because its marks deviate — as when a river swells from damming, ants move from a disturbed nest, or a peacock's cry is imitated — is answered: the marks arising in those ways (a partial swelling, flight from fear, mere similarity) are different things from the genuine marks.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 2.1.37.

paraphrase: Knowledge of things from words comes about through the capacity of the instruction of a reliable person.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 2.1.52. Part of the section arguing that verbal testimony is not a kind of inference.

paraphrase: The understanding of meaning from words rests on convention (samaya), not on a natural connection; and there is no fixed rule (of words and meanings) across particular communities.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 2.1.55.

paraphrase: (An opponent:) the Veda is not a means of knowledge because it has the faults of falsehood, self-contradiction and repetition. (Reply:) not so — (failure of a rite's result) is due to defects in the action, the agent or the means.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 2.1.57.

paraphrase: Vedic statements are employed as injunction (vidhi), explanatory statement (arthavāda) and restatement (anuvāda): an injunction enjoins; arthavāda is praise, blame, (report of) another's practice and (report of) ancient precedent; restatement is the repetition of what has been enjoined.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 2.1.62.

paraphrase: And its (the Veda's) validity — like the validity of mantras and of Āyurveda — is due to the validity (reliability) of the reliable ones (āpta).

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 2.1.68.

paraphrase: (An opponent:) the means of knowledge are not four, since tradition (aitihya), presumption (arthāpatti), inclusion (sambhava) and absence (abhāva) are also valid. (Reply:) this does not refute the four, since tradition is not different from verbal testimony, and presumption, inclusion and absence are not different from inference.

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. paraphrase: Whether cognition (buddhi) is eternal is examined: the argument that it is eternal because objects are recognized is rejected as assuming what is to be proved; cognitions arise successively and cease.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Bhāṣya on 3.2.1 names the opponent's view as Sāṃkhya: 'the buddhi, the inner instrument of the puruṣa, is eternal'.

paraphrase: (The momentarist holds that) even a crystal is not a ground (for recognizing one enduring thing), since individual things are momentary, arising and ceasing one after another. (Reply:) since there is no reason for such a universal rule, one should accept things as they are seen; and causes of origination and destruction are observed (only where things arise and perish).
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 3.2.10 reads: sphaṭike api aparāparotpatteḥ kṣaṇikatvāt vyaktīnām ahetuḥ; 3.2.11: niyamahetvabhāvāt yathādarśanam abhyanujñā. paraphrase: Undertaking and desisting belong to the knower, since they are caused by desire and aversion; the objections from the movements of material things are answered, and desire and the rest are shown not to belong to the mind, for the reasons given, because of its dependence, and because (otherwise) one would reap what one had not done.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 3.2.35.

paraphrase: (To the objection that) several actions are seen to occur at once, (it is replied that) they are apprehended so, like the circle seen when a firebrand is whirled, because of the (mind's) swift movement.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Taranatha edition (GRETIL Nyāyabhāṣya e-text) numbers this sūtra 3.2.59.

paraphrase: Karma is the cause both of the body's arising and of its connection (with a particular self); rival accounts of embodiment are examined and rejected — the last because it would entail reaping what one has not done (akṛtābhyāgama).
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. paraphrase: The faults form three groups — attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa) and delusion (moha) — because (the other faults) are included in these.

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: The view that an existent arises from non-existence — because (a sprout) appears only after (the seed) is destroyed — is rejected: it defeats itself, nothing is produced from what has been destroyed, and (the seed's destruction) merely precedes in the order of events.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: Īśvara is (said to be) the cause, since human action is seen to be (at times) fruitless; (it is objected that) without human action no fruit arises; (and answered that) this is no (valid) reason, since (the fruit) is brought about by Him.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 4.1.19 reads: īśvaraḥ kāraṇam puruṣakarmāphalyadarśanāt. Commentators differ on whether 4.1.19 states the siddhānta or a view the section qualifies; the Bhāṣya takes Īśvara to assist human effort (tea:nyaya-bhasya:4.1.21).

paraphrase: The view that everything is impermanent, since everything has the nature of arising and perishing, is rejected: (if impermanence is permanent) not everything is impermanent; the reply that impermanence perishes along with things, as fire perishes after burning its fuel, does not remove the permanent, which cannot be denied since things are settled as they are apprehended.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: The view that everything is eternal, because the five elements are eternal, is rejected, since the causes of origination and destruction are observed.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: The view that everything is non-existence, since things are established as the mutual non-existence of one another, is rejected: things are established by their own nature (svabhāva); the rejoinder that nothing is established by its own nature because everything is relative is unsound, being self-defeating.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 4.1.37 reads: sarvam abhāvo bhāveṣvitaretarābhāvasiddheḥ; 4.1.38: na svabhāvasiddherbhāvānām.

paraphrase: (The fruit, before it is produced,) is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both, because existent and non-existent are opposed; (it comes to be) because production and destruction are seen; but it is established by cognition (to have been) non-existent (before).
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 4.1.48 reads: nāsanna sanna sadasat sadasator vaidharmyāt; 4.1.50: buddhisiddhaṃ tu tadasat. The question is about the fruit of action (e.g. of a rite) before it arises; the passage is a locus of the Nyāya doctrine that effects do not pre-exist.

paraphrase: Birth itself is pain, because it is bound up with manifold affliction.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: (To the objection that birth is not only pain, since pleasure also occurs in between, it is replied that) the denial fails: for one who experiences (pleasure) affliction does not cease, owing to the fault of seeking (it); and pleasure is imagined in what is a variety of pain.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: (An opponent:) there is no liberation, because one is bound throughout life by debts, afflictions and (enjoined) activity. (Reply:) the word 'debt' is used there in a secondary sense, as a restatement serving praise and blame; the denial fails because (the sacred fires) are placed within the self (by the renunciant); and ...
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 4.1.59 reads: ṛṇakleśapravṛttyanubandhād apavargābhāvaḥ. The Bhāṣya refers the debts to the Vedic statement that a brāhmaṇa is born with three debts and answers with the doctrine of the life-stages; details of 4.1.61–62 are uncertain in this skeleton.

paraphrase: Liberation (is possible), because for one in deep sleep, when there are no dreams, there is no affliction.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit

paraphrase: (To the objection that) the stream of afflictions is natural (and so endless, it is replied that) even what is beginningless — like the prior absence of a thing — can end; and attachment and the rest are caused by (false) mental construction (saṅkalpa).
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 4.1.68 reads: na saṅkalpanimittatvācca rāgādīnām.

paraphrase: Through knowledge of the truth about the causes of the faults, the I-notion (ahaṅkāra) ceases.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: Objects such as colour, when falsely constructed (saṅkalpakṛta), are the causes of the faults.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: But the cause of these is the (false) notion of the whole (avayavy-abhimāna).

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: Doubt about the existence of the whole is raised and settled; the objections that a whole can reside in its parts neither wholly nor partly, and that it is like a mass of hair seen by one with defective sight, are answered; and the objection that division would go on until everything is dissolved is met: (division) does not end in dissolution, because atoms exist.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: There is no dissolution (into nothing), because atoms exist.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: Or: (the atom is) beyond the truṭi.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. The Bhāṣya takes truṭi as the smallest perceptible particle; the atom lies beyond it.

paraphrase: Objections that atoms must have parts — because ākāśa penetrates them, or else ākāśa is not all-pervading; because what has form has shape and conjunction — are answered: 'inside' and 'outside' apply only to effects made of other causes; ākāśa is all-pervading, non-obstructing and non-resisting; and the denial of partless atoms would lead to an infinite regress, which is untenable.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering.

paraphrase: (An opponent:) when things are analysed by the intellect their real nature is not found, as a cloth is not found when its threads are pulled out. (Reply:) this reason defeats itself; (the whole) is not apprehended apart (from the parts) because it depends on them; things are known through the means of knowledge; and (the opponent's thesis fails) whether he admits the means of knowledge or not.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 4.2.26 reads: buddhyā vivecanāttu bhāvānāṃ yāthātmyānupalabdhistantvapakarṣaṇe paṭasadbhāvānupalabdhivat tadanupalabdhiḥ.

paraphrase: (An opponent:) this notion of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge is like the notion of objects in a dream; or like magic, a city of the gandharvas, or a mirage.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. Reported view of an opponent (commentators identify idealist Buddhists) as stated in the Nyāya Sūtra. 4.2.31: svapnaviṣayābhimānavadayaṃ pramāṇaprameyābhimānaḥ; 4.2.32: māyāgandharvanagaramṛgatṛṣṇikāvadvā.

paraphrase: (Reply:) this is unproven for lack of a reason; the notion of dream-objects is like memory and imagination; false cognition is destroyed by knowledge of the truth, as the notion of dream-objects is destroyed on waking; (false cognition requires) causes that are found to exist; and false cognition is of two kinds, as it concerns the real thing and what is superimposed on it.
notes: Sūtra number and wording checked against two local e-texts (DCS; sanskrit/raw_etexts nyAya-shAstram/nyayasutra.md), which agree; this unit uses their numbering. 4.2.35 reads: mithyopalabdher vināśastattvajñānāt svapnaviṣayābhimānapraṇāśavat pratibodhe. The gloss of 4.2.37 follows the Bhāṣya and is approximate.

paraphrase: (Knowledge of truth arises) from the repeated practice of a particular samādhi.

original.edition: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit
original.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

paraphrase: The points of defeat are: abandoning the proposition, shifting the proposition, contradicting the proposition, renouncing the proposition, shifting the reason, irrelevance, meaninglessness, unintelligibility, incoherence, wrong order, saying too little, saying too much, repetition, failure to restate, ignorance, non-ingenuity, evasion, admission of the opponent's charge, overlooking what should be censured, censuring what should not be censured, deviating from one's tenet, and the pseudo-reasons.
